newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says he in charge, backs Lebed on Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says he in charge, backs Lebed on Chechnya.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin hit back on Thursday at rivals who want him to resign because of ill health, saying he was in complete charge and that it was too soon to take his picture down from office walls.

Speaking clearly from hospital in a short radio address, Yeltsin backed beleagured security tsar Alexander Lebed over a controversial Chechen peace deal, hours before new talks between Russian and separatist leaders.

Lebed and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin were due to meet Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, who flew in to Moscow form southern Russia, to try to strengthen the faltering deal signed on August 31.

"I am in touch with what is going on in the country. I am helped by a strong team of professionals," Yeltsin said in a speech apparently recorded in Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital where he is preparing for a heart operation.

Scoffing at talk that he was too ill to rule the country, he added: "I said before the elections and repeat now -- don't rush to change the portraits. The country has a president and an active president at that!".
The 65-year-old president's main aim was clearly to reassure the nation of almost 150 million that he is in charge and robust enough to have the planned bypass operation in six to 10 weeks.

He also sought to play down talk of chaos and disarray in his absence from the Kremlin. His opponents said in parliament on Wednesday that the country was leaderless and demanded swift action to put things in order.
Yeltsin applauded Lebed, who has also came under fire in parliament over the peace deal and has been widely accused of fighting hard for power in Yeltsin's absence.
"My aide Alexander Lebed fulfilled my instruction and stopped the military conflict (in Chechnya)," Yeltsin said, adding that a lot yet had to be done to implement the deal.

The president also had praise for the Kremlin administration, headed by chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, and the government of Chernomyrdin. The two men are widely reported to be Lebed's rivals for power.
Yeltsin was due to meet Lebed later on Thursday to discuss the situation in Chechnya.
The president also met Defence Minister Igor Rodionov earlier on Thursday on financing of the cash-strapped army.
"I am very worried about the situation in the armed forces...This situation must not be dragged out any longer," Yeltsin said in the radio address.
He said a meeting of defence officials to be chaired by Chernomyrdin on Friday should come up with "concrete decisions" on the future of the armed forces.
It was not clear if Yeltsin discussed Chechnya with Rodionov.

A ceasefire agreed under the August 31 peace deal in Chechnya has held, but the planned withdrawal of Russian troops from the region is proceeding slowly. Prisoner exchanges have also not gone as well as planned.
Critics say the separatist rebels, who want indepedence from Russia, have got away with too much.

Chernomyrdin has previously played go-between with Lebed over Chechnya. But he has given Lebed's deal a lukewarm response and it is not clear what his renewed involvement in the peace process will achieve.
Chernomyrdin, 58, has taken over some of Yeltsin's powers in the run-up to the president's heart bypass operation.

Opposition groups were expected to hold rallies around Moscow's television tower on Thursday to mark the 1993 confrontation between the security forces and supporters of hardline parliamentarians Yeltsin accused of blocking reforms.
More than 120 people were killed in the clashes and in subsequent battles around the White House parliament building before Yeltsin defeated his political foes.
